nature-eco-673.title: Detritivores: the first stage of rot
nature-eco-673.text:
Why does a forest floor not bury itself in dead leaves? Part of the answer is a crowd of small animals that eat the debris. A detritivore is a heterotroph that gets its nutrients by eating detritus: decomposing plant and animal parts and faeces. Millipedes, springtails, woodlice, dung flies, slugs, earthworms and sea cucumbers all work this way.

They swallow lumps of matter. Bacteria, fungi and protists, the {{ref:nature-eco-340}}, instead absorb nutrients at a molecular scale. The animals do the first stage of remineralization by fragmenting dead plant matter, so the microbes can do the second. Together they return carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, calcium and potassium to the soil.

The job once went undone. In the Carboniferous, fungi and bacteria had not yet evolved the ability to digest lignin, so large deposits of dead plant tissue built up and later became fossil fuels. Feeding on sediment has a cost: some detritivores incidentally concentrate toxic pollutants.

nature-eco-676.title: The soil food web
nature-eco-676.text:
Beneath a single footstep lies a community that spans a wide range of sizes, from nematodes under 0.1 mm to earthworms over 2 mm. This is the soil food web: the organisms living all or part of their lives in {{ref:nature-eco-387}}, and the feeding links that move energy through it. Plant roots feed it by exuding acids, sugars and enzymes into the rhizosphere, and bacteria and fungi end each chain by breaking dead matter into simple nutrients.

Soil ecologists found that omnivory is common and that long, complex chains resist drying, freezing and fumigation. That contradicts May's models, which predicted that complexity destabilizes webs. Some links defy simple control models too: isopods enrich their own faecal pellets with microbes and eat them again, a mutualism called an external rumen.

nature-eco-745.title: Natural selection: why the better adapted leave more offspring
nature-eco-745.text:
Natural selection is the differential survival and reproduction of individuals owing to differences in their relative fitness. It is a key mechanism of evolution, the change in the heritable traits of a population or species over generations. Darwin set out the theory in 1859 to explain adaptation and speciation: individuals best adapted to their environments are more likely to survive and reproduce.

The logic needs only one ingredient. Heritable variation must raise an individual's lifetime reproductive rate. When such variation passes from parent to offspring, reproduction becomes differential, and the next generation differs from the last.

Selection is not always directional or adaptive. It often maintains the status quo by eliminating less fit variants. It also acts today: misuse of antibiotics has selected for resistant microbes, such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), called a superbug.

Integration with Mendel's laws in the early 20th-century modern synthesis led scientists to accept natural selection. It remains the foundation of evolutionary theory.

nature-eco-746.title: Fitness: reproductive success, not long life
nature-eco-746.text: "Survival of the fittest" hides a much subtler meaning. In modern evolutionary theory, fitness is how successful an organism is at reproducing, not how long it lives. The concept is central to {{ref:nature-eco-745}}. Traits that raise reproductive success are selected for, and those that lower it are selected against.

nature-eco-747.title: Kinds of natural selection
nature-eco-747.text:
Selection can be sorted in several ways: by its effect on a trait, on genetic diversity, by life cycle stage, by unit of selection, or by resource competed for. Stabilizing selection holds a trait at an optimum, while directional selection favours extreme values. Purifying selection removes genetic variation; balancing selection maintains it through negative frequency-dependent selection.

Viability selection raises survival probability, and fecundity selection raises reproductive rate. Sexual selection is competition for mates. It typically proceeds via fecundity selection, sometimes at the expense of viability.

nature-eco-751.title: Genetic drift: evolution by chance
nature-eco-751.text:
Not all evolution is a contest of better against worse. Genetic drift is the change in the frequency of an existing allele in a population due to chance. Drift can remove alleles completely, cutting genetic variation, or push a rare allele to fixation, where it displaces all others.

The arithmetic is blunt. Random sampling can remove an allele but not replace it, so drift drives a population toward genetic uniformity. An allele at frequency 1 is fixed, and at 0 it is lost. With drift alone, an allele's chance of eventual fixation equals its frequency, and fixation comes much faster in smaller populations. Calculations use the effective population size, which is smaller than the total population.

Unlike {{ref:nature-eco-745}}, drift has no direction toward adaptation. It acts on genotype frequencies regardless of phenotypic effect, and it works together with selection, mutation and migration.

How much it matters is a long argument. Fisher thought drift played at most a minor role. Kimura's 1968 neutral theory claimed that most spread of genetic change comes from drift acting on neutral mutations. Biologists have debated since the mid 20th century how much evolution is driven by drift versus selection, and the question is not settled.

nature-eco-748.title: Gene flow: genes on the move between populations
nature-eco-748.text:
Gene flow, also called migration, is the transfer of genetic material from one population to another. Its power is easy to underrate. If the rate is high enough, two populations share equivalent allele frequencies and count as one effective population. One migrant per generation is enough to prevent divergence driven by {{ref:nature-eco-751}}.

High gene flow reduces genetic differentiation and can constrain speciation and range expansion. It can also add novel variants under positive selection, a process called adaptive introgression. Researchers estimate it directly from dispersal and reproductive success, or indirectly by comparing allele frequencies; with one migrant per generation, FST equals 0.2.

Barriers stop it. They can be physical, as in allopatric speciation, or reproductive, as in sympatric speciation. The Great Wall of China has hindered gene flow in native plants. Hybridization with introduced species can swamp a rare species' gene pool, when introgression replaces its alleles with an invader's.

The effects depend on context. Gene flow can enhance a population's fitness or have negative consequences.

nature-eco-760.title: Population viability analysis: forecasting extinction risk
nature-eco-760.text:
How likely is a population to vanish within a set number of years? Population viability analysis is a species-specific risk assessment method in conservation biology that gives that probability. It combines species characteristics and environmental variability to forecast population health and extinction risk, and each analysis is built for one target population. Managers use it to judge urgency of recovery, find key life stages, compare management options and assess impacts of habitat loss.

Mark Shaffer's 1978 grizzly bear model at Yellowstone calculated extinction probabilities and a minimum viable population size. US use grew with the Endangered Species Act of 1973. One analysis of Fender's blue butterfly found it more at risk than thought and located key recovery sites. Another, of the Santa Catalina island fox, found it highly susceptible to catastrophes more often than once every 20 years.

Critics note that a precise forecast T years ahead may need five to ten times T years of data, and suitable data exist for only 2% of threatened birds. Retrospective tests show projections are accurate with sound or long-term data. Its value lies more in assessing threats than in making long-term categorical predictions, and debates over its proper uses remain unresolved.

nature-eco-754.title: Life history theory: how organisms spend a lifetime
nature-eco-754.text:
Why does one animal mature quickly and breed often while another waits and breeds rarely? Life history theory is a framework for studying such diversity and the causes and results of variation in organisms' life cycles. A life history strategy is the age- and stage-specific pattern and timing of events such as maturation, reproduction and death, shaped by the organism's physical and ecological environment.

The theory arose in the 1950s. It addresses body size, age of maturation, number of offspring and life span. Fitness is often assessed as the number of descendants over a lifetime, mainly survivorship and reproductive rate.

Environments in which resources, hazards and competitors fluctuate rapidly select for earlier reproduction and more offspring. High mortality rates, the usual result of an unpredictable environment, typically go with earlier maturity than low mortality rates. r/K selection theory frames the central trade-off: number of offspring against timing of reproduction.

nature-eco-753.title: The intermediate disturbance hypothesis
nature-eco-753.text:
Diversity peaks, the hypothesis says, when things are shaken up a moderate amount. The intermediate disturbance hypothesis holds that local species diversity is highest when ecological disturbance is neither too rare nor too frequent. At low disturbance, competitive species push others to extinction. At high disturbance, all species risk extinction.

At intermediate levels, species of early and late successional stages coexist, because moderate disturbance prevents interspecific competition from running to exclusion. K-selected species dominate stable ecosystems, and r-selected species colonize recently cleared areas. Occasional disturbance lets both live together. It is a nonequilibrium model, with Connell usually cited as its founder, and its hump-backed graph shows diversity against disturbance.

The idea is contested. The terms intermediate and disturbance are ambiguous: what counts depends on the system's disturbance history and on whether frequency, extent, intensity or duration is evaluated. The marine Menge-Sutherland model also showed a discrepancy with it.

nature-eco-749.title: Assisted gene flow for conservation
nature-eco-749.text: Conservationists can imitate nature's migrants. Assisted gene flow is a management strategy that conserves at-risk species by simulating natural {{ref:nature-eco-748}}, moving individuals or gametes between populations. Moving individuals within a species' existing range can help it adapt to projected local climate conditions. It can introduce pre-adapted genotypes or raise the frequency of existing climate-adapted ones, and it suits any species whose habitat will change greatly.

nature-eco-750.title: Cities and gene flow: fragmentation or connection
nature-eco-750.text: Cities can split populations or join them. Two models describe how urbanization affects {{ref:nature-eco-748}}: habitat fragmentation, which lowers genetic diversity, and urban facilitation, which connects populations. Facilitation reduces isolation and brings previously separated species into contact, directly or indirectly. Whether corridors work depends on species' dispersal abilities and their adaptiveness to anthropogenic structures.

nature-eco-752.title: Population bottlenecks and the founder effect
nature-eco-752.text:
A population bottleneck is a sharp contraction in population size over a short time due to a random environmental event. Survival in a true bottleneck is random, not improved by any genetic advantage. Allele frequencies can therefore change radically independent of selection, and inbreeding increases afterward.

The founder effect is a special case. A small group splits off and forms a new population whose alleles grossly misrepresent the original population. Such effects can shape a small colony's genetics far into the future, as with the recessive Ellis-Van Creveld allele in the 1744 Amish migration to Pennsylvania.

nature-eco-756.title: Capital and income breeding
nature-eco-756.text: Capital and income breeding describe how organisms finance and time breeding with resources. Capital breeders pay with resources gathered earlier and breed once body condition passes a threshold. Income breeders use resources generated during breeding. The two form a spectrum rather than a strict dichotomy.

nature-eco-755.title: Life history trade-offs
nature-eco-755.text:
No organism can do everything. Life history trade-offs arise because an organism has limited energy and must choose among growth, reproduction and survival. Examples are the trade-off between maximizing body size and lifespan, and between offspring size and number.

Trade-offs limit adaptation and fitness. Without them a hypothetical Darwinian demon would have the highest fitness. Populations can reach an optimal strategy that maximizes fitness, which depends on how resources are allocated.

nature-eco-757.title: The paradox of enrichment
nature-eco-757.text:
Feeding the prey can doom the predator. The paradox of enrichment is the idea that increasing the food available to a prey species can destabilize the predator's population. Michael Rosenzweig coined it in 1971. Enrichment was modelled as a higher prey carrying capacity, which can make the equilibrium unstable, usually giving a limit cycle. The predator boom can crash and may lead to local eradication or extinction of the predator.

Past a critical carrying capacity the system undergoes a Hopf bifurcation. The result is counterintuitive, hence 'paradox'. Support comes mainly from small laboratory experiments, with limited field support. Destabilisation need not occur with inedible, invulnerable or unpalatable prey, a ratio-dependent functional response such as the Arditi-Ginzburg model, spatial heterogeneity, inducible defense, or density-dependent predator mortality.

nature-eco-758.title: Population pyramids: reading a population's age shape
nature-eco-758.text:
A population pyramid is a graph of a population's distribution by age group and sex, usually for a country or region. Males are conventionally on the left and females on the right, with bars in absolute numbers or percentages. In ecology it shows a population's age distribution, hinting at reproductive capability and likelihood of continuation.

A broad base signals fertility above replacement, and the shape also reveals the age-dependency ratio of those too young or old to work. Pyramids fall into three types: stationary, with births and deaths roughly balanced; expansive, wide at young ages; and constrictive, narrowed at the bottom. Their shape tracks the demographic transition: more developed countries sit in stages three to five, least developed in stages one and two.

nature-eco-759.title: Youth bulge: when the young outnumber everyone
nature-eco-759.text:
A youth bulge is a type of expansive {{ref:nature-eco-758}} with a large share of young people. Large cohorts entering the labor force strain economy and polity, creating unemployment unless opportunities arise fast enough. If they do, a demographic dividend accrues as workers outweigh dependents.

In developing countries youth bulges go with higher unemployment and a heightened risk of violence and instability. A 2016 study found they raise the chance of non-ethnic civil wars but not ethnic ones. Suggested policy responses include creating jobs, improving family planning and reducing infant mortality. In the Middle East and North Africa about 65% of the population is under 25, and the region's youth bulge has been called a demographic gift that could fuel growth if harnessed.
